teacherGuide.overview: Explains friction and air resistance as forces that oppose motion, how they are reduced, how magnetic levitation removes rolling friction, and what the hyperloop story shows about turning physics into engineering.
learningGoals: Define friction and air resistance and give examples of each.
Describe ways of reducing friction and air resistance.
State the rule for magnetic poles and explain how a maglev train floats.
Explain why a sound scientific idea may still fail as a working system.

beforeReading: Ask learners to rub their palms together for ten seconds and describe what they feel and why.
whileReading: Pause on Page 3 with two bar magnets: let learners feel like poles repel and unlike poles attract.
afterReading: Slide a book across a desk, then roll it over three round pencils. Compare the force needed and explain the difference.
discussion: The hyperloop company spent a great deal of money and then closed. Was the effort wasted?
reflection: Where in your home or community would less friction save effort or fuel?

mathsExtension.task: Accra to Kumasi is 250 km. How long would the journey take at 600 km/h? Give your answer in minutes.
The test pod reached 387 km/h. The design speed was about 1,200 km/h. What fraction of the design speed was reached?
mathsExtension.answer: 387 ÷ 1,200 is about one third (32 per cent).

mathsExtension.task: A coach takes 7 hours to cover 250 km. How many times faster than the coach is a 600 km/h maglev?
mathsExtension.answer: The coach averages about 36 km/h; 600 ÷ 36 is about 17 times faster.

support: Provide picture cards of everyday situations for learners to sort into “friction helps” and “friction wastes energy”.
stretch: Find out why air resistance increases so quickly with speed, and why racing cyclists ride close behind one another.

factCheck.claim: Japan’s L0 Series maglev train reached 603 km/h in 2015; Hyperloop One reached 387 km/h uncrewed (2017) and 172 km/h with passengers (2020) before closing at the end of 2023.
factCheck.explanation: Hyperloop One test speeds (387 km/h; 172 km/h with passengers) and closure at the end of 2023 checked alongside the Central Japan Railway maglev speed record (603 km/h, April 2015).
factCheck.reference: Central Japan Railway Company (2015); Virgin Hyperloop test reports (2017, 2020).

pronunciation.guidance: Ghanaians often say "uh-KRAH" (stress on the second syllable).
